transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Good morning. Today I want to examine the placebo effect, which is one of the most fascinating, and most misunderstood, phenomena in medicine. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, and the placebo effect refers to the improvement that patients sometimes experience after taking it.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The earliest systematic study was carried out in 1955 by Henry Beecher, a doctor who reviewed fifteen trials and concluded that about thirty-five per cent of patients improved after receiving a placebo. That figure was quoted for decades. We now know it was misleading. Beecher didn't separate the placebo effect from other explanations, such as the natural course of the illness. Many patients recover with no treatment at all, so improvement after a sugar pill doesn't prove that the pill caused it.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: More careful research has produced a more nuanced picture. The placebo effect is real, but it's strongest for conditions that depend on perception, such as pain, nausea and fatigue. It's much weaker, or absent, for conditions that can be measured objectively, such as blood cell counts or tumour size. In other words, a placebo may make you feel better without changing the underlying disease.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: How does it work? One mechanism is expectation. When people believe that a treatment will help, the brain releases chemicals such as endorphins, which reduce pain. Brain scans show that the same regions are active as when a real painkiller is taken. A second mechanism is conditioning. If you have repeatedly taken a pill that relieved your headache, your body may learn to respond to the pill itself.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Some surprising findings have emerged. Larger pills work better than small ones, injections work better than tablets, and brand-name packaging produces stronger effects than plain packaging, even if the contents are identical. Most remarkably, in a few studies, patients were told honestly that they were receiving a placebo, and some still improved. Researchers called this open-label placebo, although the sample sizes were small, and the findings need replication.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: This raises an ethical question. Should doctors ever prescribe placebos? Deceiving patients seems to violate trust, and most professional guidelines forbid it. Yet surveys suggest that a surprising proportion of doctors admit to giving treatments they believe have only a placebo benefit, such as vitamins. A reasonable position may be that the placebo effect is best harnessed indirectly: by taking time to listen, explaining treatments clearly and showing confidence in the plan, a doctor can improve outcomes without deception.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: To sum up, the placebo effect is neither magic nor a myth. It tells us that the experience of illness is shaped by the mind as well as the body. For next week, please read the article by Kaptchuk and prepare a brief critique of its methodology.
